title: Tunable GPU throttles and priority backfill for hosted API capacity exhaustion
creator: Aisha Patel
description:
Summary: After the hosted API GPU exhaustion incident on 2026-02-25 we observed extended queue growth caused by slow-moving large-batch inference jobs that saturated GPU pools and blocked short-latency requests. This ticket captures an actionable plan to implement tunable admission throttles, priority-aware backfill, and graceful preemption so we can (1) limit queue amplification, (2) protect latency-sensitive traffic, and (3) provide predictable recovery behavior during capacity events.

Observed behavior & root cause: During the incident a minority of submissions used large effective batch sizes and long sequence lengths, causing per-request GPU time to spike. Autoscaler reacted slowly because scale-up signals were tied to average GPU utilization over a minute; meanwhile the request admission controller admitted all requests, which allowed queue length to grow until the scheduler hit out-of-memory / kernel timeouts and began dropping/ retrying. The combination of: (a) coarse autoscaler signals, (b) lack of admission throttles by request cost, and (c) no preemption/backfill policy for short jobs led to prolonged customer impact.

Goals: 1) Add a tunable admission controller that considers per-request estimated GPU cost (tokens * seq_len * model_cost_factor) and enforces pool-level capacity thresholds; 2) Implement priority backfill: keep a reserved token for latency-sensitive routes and allow preemption of queued expensive requests when high-priority short requests arrive; 3) Improve autoscaler and scale-up triggers to be sensitive to queue composition and tail latencies; 4) Provide observability and runbook updates so on-call can make data-driven decisions during future events.

Proposal: Phase 1 (safety net, short): - Add admission-limit config per GPU pool (soft_limit, hard_limit) and per-route priority weights. - Reject / 429 expensive requests when soft_limit exceeded (with helpful retry-after header) and record metrics for rejected cost. - Emit new metrics: pool_estimated_cost_in_flight, queue_cost_lead, high_priority_drops. Phase 2 (runtime changes): - Implement backfill: a preemptive queue comparator that can evict the oldest or highest-cost queued requests to free space for high-priority short requests. - Add preemption hooks to the scheduler to checkpoint and surface partial progress to clients (where applicable) and log eviction reasons. Phase 3 (autoscaler/operational): - Tune autoscaler to weight queue_cost_lead, 95th percentile token-processing-time, and rapid scale-up policy (add single-step burst nodes). - Update runbooks with playbook steps, thresholds, and rollback criteria.

Acceptance criteria: - Admission controller in prod can be toggled per-pool via Console; default soft_limit prevents >30% queue growth for mixed workloads in synthetic tests. - Priority backfill allows <1% of high-priority requests to observe 429s during synthetic burst tests while keeping total error rate within SLA. - New metrics appear in Grafana and are used by the autoscaler; runbook updated and validated in on-call run.

Out of scope: Full KV-cache-aware cost estimation (follow-up), predictive admission using ML.

Success metrics: Reduced time-to-recovery (TTR) in replayed incidents from median 22m to <8m, reduced P95 latency impact for high-priority routes by 60% during bursts, and decreased dropped short requests by 80%.

2026-03-06 — Daniel Cho: Spike completed — estimated_cost function (tokens * seq_len * model_factor) implemented in runtime-sim; results show high correlation with observed GPU ms. Adding margin factor for accelerator variance.

2026-03-08 — Priya Iyer (SRE): Integrated new metrics into dev Grafana dashboard (link: https://grafana.redwood.internal/d/GPUEstimated/hosted-capacity). Found one alert gap which we added to alerting policy.
